summary: A landlocked region in the central Balkans whose inhabitants are mainly Albanians; the 1389 Battle of Kosovo and the medieval Serbian monasteries have made it the core of Serbian national memory. After the 1998-1999 war it was placed under United Nations administration, and in 2008 it declared independence from Serbia; international recognition remains disputed to this day.

ranking.name: Islam (Sunni)
ranking.description: From the late 14th century the Ottoman Empire gradually expanded into Kosovo; after the 1389 Battle of Kosovo the Serbian lords became vassals, and in the mid-15th century the area was formally incorporated into the empire. Converting to Islam exempted people from the poll tax on non-Muslims (jizya) and brought opportunities for official and military posts, and in the 17th-18th centuries many Albanians converted, making Sunni Islam the faith of the great majority. In the 2011 census about 95.6 percent of the population registered as Muslim, and Ottoman buildings such as the Sinan Pasha Mosque in Prizren remain landmarks of the city today.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: Catholicism was one of the traditional faiths of the Albanians before Ottoman rule, and a minority community survived the wave of conversions, concentrated mainly around Prizren, Gjakova and Letnica; some families outwardly converted to Islam while secretly maintaining Catholic belief and were known as "crypto-Catholics." Because Mother Teresa, who came from an Albanian family, is a national symbol, a cathedral named after her was completed in Pristina in 2017.

ranking.name: Eastern Orthodoxy
ranking.description: Eastern Orthodoxy is the faith of the Kosovo Serbs. In the 14th century this was the center of the Serbian kingdom, in 1346 Peć became the seat of the Serbian Patriarch, and medieval buildings such as Visoki Dečani Monastery were inscribed on UNESCO's World Heritage List in 2004. After the 1999 war large numbers of Serbs left, and those who remain are concentrated mainly around Mitrovica in the north and in scattered enclaves; because the northern Serb community boycotted the 2011 census, the Orthodox share in the census is only about 1.5 percent, and the actual number is probably greater.

religion.background: Kosovo was already Christianized in the Roman and Byzantine periods, and in the 12th-14th centuries belonged to the Serbian kingdom; the Patriarchate of Peć and a large number of monasteries led the Serbs to regard it as the "cradle of the nation." After the 1389 Battle of Kosovo Ottoman power entered, and by the 19th century Albanian Muslims had become the majority of the population, with religious and ethnic lines roughly overlapping: Albanians were mostly Muslims and Serbs Orthodox. Under Yugoslav communism (1945-1991) religion was suppressed by the state and society became secularized, so many Kosovars today, though identifying as Muslim, live fairly secular daily lives. During the 1998-1999 war both mosques and Orthodox churches were damaged, and in the riots of March 2004 dozens of Orthodox churches and monasteries were burned, so the protection of religious heritage remains a sensitive issue.

language.official: The official languages are Albanian and Serbian; Turkish, Bosnian and Romani have official status in some municipalities.

ranking.name: Albanian
ranking.description: Albanians gradually became the majority of Kosovo's population from the Ottoman period, and in the 2011 census about 94 percent of the population had Albanian as their mother tongue. The northern Gheg dialect is used in daily life, but the 1968 Pristina linguistic conference decided to adopt the standard language common with Albania (based on the southern Tosk dialect). After the Serbian government closed Albanian-language schools in 1990, Kosovars ran a "parallel education system" with classes held in private homes, so the language became a symbol of national resistance.

ranking.name: Serbian
ranking.description: Serbian is the language Serbs have used here since the Middle Ages, and was also the main language of administration and education in the Yugoslav period. After the 1999 war large numbers of Serbs left, and speakers are concentrated in the north in places such as Mitrovica and Zvečan and in the Serb enclaves of the south. The 2008 constitution still lists it together with Albanian as an official language; because the northern Serbs boycotted the 2011 census, the share of about 1.6 percent in the census clearly underestimates the actual number of speakers.

ranking.name: Bosnian
ranking.description: Bosnian speakers are mainly Muslim Slavs (Bosniaks), concentrated in the Prizren and Peć areas, along with the Gorani, who speak a related dialect in the Gora mountain area in the south. In religion they are Muslim like the Albanians, but in language they are close to Serbian, reflecting the history of Slavic conversion during the Ottoman period. The 2006 Law on the Use of Languages gave it official status in municipalities where the population reaches a certain share.

ranking.name: Turkish
ranking.description: Turkish is a legacy of nearly five hundred years of Ottoman rule, when it was the language of administration, commerce and the urban elite, and upper-class families in Prizren long conversed in Turkish. Today those with Turkish as their mother tongue make up about 1 percent, concentrated in Prizren and in Mamuša in the south (where most residents are ethnically Turkish). It has official status in these municipalities, and many Albanian words also come from Turkish.

language.history: In the Middle Ages Kosovo was the heart of the Serbian kingdom, and Church Slavonic and Serbian were the languages of religion and written culture at that time. During the Ottoman period Turkish became the language of administration, while Albanian was used mainly orally; the League of Prizren, founded in Prizren in 1878, promoted the Albanian national movement and also stimulated demands for writing and education in the native language. In the Yugoslav period Kosovo gained autonomy under the 1974 constitution, and the University of Pristina, founded in 1970, taught in Albanian and trained a large intelligentsia; after Milošević abolished autonomy in 1989, Albanian-language education was pushed aside. The constitution after independence in 2008 provides that Albanian and Serbian are both official languages and guarantees the languages of other minorities.

ranking.name: Flija
ranking.description: A thin batter of flour, water and salt is brushed layer by layer onto a large round baking pan, with cream or butter spread between the layers, and baked for several hours under a metal lid (saç) heated with charcoal from above; the result resembles a many-layered crepe and is often eaten with yogurt, pickles or honey.
ranking.history: Flija is a traditional dish of Kosovo and the highlands of northern Albania, and its method reflects the diet of mountain herders based on flour and dairy products. It is not baked in an oven but outdoors under a metal lid heated with charcoal, layer by layer, which takes two or three hours at a time, so it is often made only when relatives and neighbors gather. Because it is time-consuming and requires a division of labor, flija is regarded in Kosovo as a symbol of hospitality and reunion, outdoor gatherings with it as the star are often held in summer, and many people still consider it the national dish of Kosovo.

ranking.name: Pite (pie)
ranking.description: Hand-rolled, paper-thin dough is layered around fillings such as white cheese, spinach, minced meat or pumpkin and baked into a large round tray; the crust is crisp, and it is often cut into pieces and eaten with yogurt for breakfast.
ranking.history: Pite belongs to the family of "börek" pastries of the Ottoman Empire and became widespread in the Balkans after the Ottoman conquest in the 15th century. Kosovars call it "pite" or "burek," and the dough is prized for being rolled paper-thin; whether it can be made well is regarded as an important skill for a housewife. Today there are specialty shops all over the streets of Pristina and Prizren, eating pite with a glass of yogurt in the morning is a common everyday breakfast, and it also often appears on the table when breaking the fast in Ramadan.

ranking.name: Qebapa (grilled minced-meat rolls)
ranking.description: Ground beef (sometimes mixed with lamb) seasoned with salt and spices is shaped into small finger-sized rolls, grilled over charcoal and served in bread with raw onion and cream cheese (kajmak).
ranking.history: Qebapa derives from the grilled-meat tradition of the Ottoman Empire; both "qebapa" and Bosnian "ćevapi" come from the word "kebab," and spread across the Balkans with Ottoman rule after the 15th century. Because Islamic dietary rules forbid pork, the Kosovo version is based on beef and lamb. It is the signature dish of city grill houses (qebaptore), and from the Yugoslav period to today it has been one of the most common inexpensive meals eaten out.

ranking.name: Stewed white beans (Tavë me fasule)
ranking.description: White kidney beans are slowly stewed with onion and paprika into a thick bean soup, often with smoked meat added for aroma, and eaten with cornbread or white bread.
ranking.history: The common bean originated in the Americas and was brought to Europe via Spain and Mediterranean trade after the 16th century, later becoming a cheap, long-keeping source of protein in the Balkans. Stewed white beans are common throughout Yugoslavia and are a regular dish in army and school canteens; Muslim families in Kosovo usually use dried beef or smoked beef in place of the pork commonly used in other regions. In winter every household cooks a big pot, and it is regarded as one of the most everyday home-cooked dishes.

ranking.name: Trileçe (three-milk cake)
ranking.description: A sponge cake is soaked in three milks, namely milk, condensed milk and cream, with a layer of caramel spread on top, and served chilled; it is moist and sweet.
ranking.history: Trileçe derives from the Latin American "tres leches" and is generally believed to have reached Albania and Kosovo only after the 1990s, quickly becoming popular. The local version adds a caramel top layer as a distinguishing feature, and "trileçe" means "three milks." After the 1999 war and after independence in 2008, with the large flow of diaspora visits and the influx of outside culture, new-style dessert shops multiplied in Pristina, and trileçe became the most popular signature dessert, reflecting the dietary changes of Kosovo's rapidly globalizing postwar society.
